unit.name: Theme C: The Existence of God & Revelation
unit.subtitle: Philosophical arguments for and against God, and the nature of revelation

lessons.title: Arguments For the Existence of God
lessons.description: Design argument, First Cause argument and argument from miracles: strengths, weaknesses and a miracle example.
lessons.content_html:
Can Reason Prove God Exists?

For centuries, philosophers and theologians have asked whether reason alone can demonstrate that God exists. Three classic arguments have shaped this debate: the Design argument, the First Cause argument, and the argument from miracles. Each attempts to move from things we can observe in the world to a conclusion about God’s existence. Each has also attracted powerful objections. This lesson explores all three, so that you can evaluate them fairly.

Key Fact

The three main arguments for God’s existence are: the Design argument (associated with William Paley, 1802), the First Cause argument (associated with Thomas Aquinas, 13th century), and the argument from miracles. All three draw on evidence from the world around us rather than from scripture alone.

The Design Argument (Teleological Argument)

The Design argument holds that the universe shows signs of purpose and order that are best explained by a designer. The philosopher William Paley presented this vividly in Natural Theology (1802) through his famous watchmaker analogy. Paley argued that if you found a watch on a heath and examined its cogs and springs working together to tell the time, you would immediately conclude the watch had a designer. The natural world, with its intricate ecosystems, the human eye, the precise conditions that allow life on Earth, shows the same complexity. Therefore, Paley reasoned, just as the watch demands a watchmaker, the universe demands a divine designer — whom Christians, Muslims, Jews and Sikhs identify as God.

Contemporary thinkers such as Richard Swinburne have developed the teleological argument, pointing to the fine-tuning of physical constants in the universe as evidence that its orderliness requires explanation. From a Christian perspective, Genesis 1 portrays God deliberately creating and ordering the world — “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). Many believers see in the structure of nature a sign of God’s creative intelligence.

Strengths: The argument is based on observable evidence. It matches the intuition many people have when they look at the natural world — that it seems designed. Philosophers such as F.R. Tennant highlighted that the universe appears fine-tuned to permit life in a way that seems too precise to be coincidence.

Weaknesses: David Hume, writing before Paley in Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, challenged the analogy: a watch is made of parts put together by human hands, but the universe is not like a watch. Hume also noted that the universe might have many designers, not one; that poor design in nature (disease, natural disasters) might suggest an imperfect or uncaring designer; and that an analogy is not proof. Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection (1859) offered an alternative explanation for biological complexity — the appearance of design can arise through random variation and the survival of organisms best adapted to their environment, without any designer being needed.

The First Cause Argument (Cosmological Argument)

Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian, developed a series of arguments for God’s existence that he presented in his major work Summa Theologiae. The second of his Five Ways addresses causation. Aquinas observed that in the world everything that exists is caused by something before it. A flame burns wood; the wood was grown from a seed; the seed came from a tree. This chain cannot go back forever — an infinite chain of causes, Aquinas argued, would never have got started. There must be a First Cause that began the chain of causation but was not itself caused. This uncaused first cause, Aquinas reasoned, is what people call God.

Islamic theology makes a similar argument: the kalam cosmological argument holds that everything that begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause outside itself, which is God. Jewish theology also holds that God is the uncaused creator (Bore olam — Creator of the universe). Across these traditions, the First Cause argument reinforces the monotheistic conviction that God exists necessarily, not contingently.

Strengths: The argument uses logical reasoning. It aligns with the Big Bang cosmological model, which suggests the universe did have a beginning. Many scientists accept that something caused the Big Bang, even if they disagree about what that something was. Philosopher Alvin Plantinga has argued that God is the only plausible candidate for a necessary, uncaused being.

Weaknesses: Bertrand Russell argued that the universe may simply exist without needing a cause — “The universe is just there, and that’s all.” If everything requires a cause, what caused God? Aquinas’s response is that God, by definition, is uncaused — a necessary being — but critics argue this is an assertion rather than a proof. The argument may also prove only that something caused the universe, not that this cause is the personal God of Christianity or Islam.

The Argument from Miracles

The third argument holds that miracles — events that seem to violate the normal laws of nature — provide evidence that a powerful God acts in the world. Aquinas defined a miracle as something done by God that nature could not do on its own. For Christians, the resurrection of Jesus is the central miracle: on the third day after his crucifixion, the Gospels record that Jesus rose from the dead (Luke 24:1–12). If this happened as reported, it represents God’s direct intervention in the physical world and is the foundation of Christian belief in eternal life.

A second widely cited example is the healing miracles attributed to the shrine at Lourdes, France, where in 1858 a young girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported a series of visions of the Virgin Mary. Since then, the Catholic Church has officially recognised 70 miraculous healings at Lourdes after rigorous medical scrutiny, including cases where patients recovered from conditions doctors could not explain. Believers argue these healings point to God’s continuing power to act in the world.

Key Fact

The argument from miracles says: if miracles occur — events that break the laws of nature — they require a supernatural cause; God is the only adequate supernatural cause; therefore God exists. The resurrection of Jesus (Luke 24) and the healings at Lourdes (from 1858) are cited as examples by Christians.

Strengths and Weaknesses of the Argument from Miracles

David Hume raised a powerful challenge in Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748). He argued that it is always more probable that the witness to a miracle was mistaken, deceived, or lying than that the laws of nature were actually broken. Hume also noted that people in many cultures report miracles on behalf of contradictory religions — they cannot all be right, which undermines the evidential value of miracle accounts. Philosophers such as J.L. Mackie developed this critique further, arguing that reliable scientific evidence for a law of nature will always outweigh the testimony of individual witnesses.

Believers respond that dismissing all miraculous reports on principle is itself a bias. They argue that where many independent witnesses report the same unexplained event, testimony deserves serious weight. From a non-religious perspective, however, humanists and atheists typically explain apparently miraculous events through unknown natural causes, misdiagnosis, spontaneous remission, or psychological factors. For humanists, the world is governed entirely by natural laws and there is no credible scientific evidence for supernatural intervention.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark ‘Explain two reasons’ question for Theme C, the mark scheme specifically requires you to refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching. This means naming a source and showing how it connects to your argument. For this topic, strong sources include Genesis 1:31 (“God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” — supporting the Design argument) or Luke 24 (the resurrection — supporting the argument from miracles). Quoting Paley or Aquinas by name and work also counts as a source of religious/philosophical teaching. Without naming a source, your answer is capped below the Mastering band regardless of how detailed the rest of your answer is.

On the 12-mark Evaluate question, you must argue both for AND against the statement and then reach a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION. Do not just describe the arguments — evaluate which side is stronger and say why. Your conclusion must be reasoned: “I conclude that the Design argument is not convincing because... however, for believers it has value because...” Without a conclusion, your answer stays in the Developing band at most.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Design argument (Paley’s watchmaker analogy) says the order and complexity of the universe implies a designer; challenged by Hume (weak analogy) and Darwin (evolution explains complexity without a designer).
  • The First Cause argument (Aquinas’s Second Way) says the chain of causation requires an uncaused First Cause — God; challenged by Russell (the universe may need no cause) and the question of who caused God.
  • The argument from miracles says events that break natural laws — such as the resurrection (Luke 24) or the healings at Lourdes — require a divine cause; challenged by Hume (witness testimony is insufficient) and naturalistic explanations from atheism and humanism.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Design argument for God's existence?
A) God must exist because everything has a cause
B) The order and complexity of the universe suggests it was designed by God
C) Miracles prove that God intervenes in the world
D) Religious experiences are proof that God is personal
practice_questions.marks: B) The order and complexity of the universe suggests it was designed by God [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the philosopher who used the watchmaker analogy to argue for God's existence.

Explain two contrasting views on whether the Design argument proves God exists.
In your answer, refer to a religious or philosophical viewpoint and a non-religious viewpoint.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark per point stated, 2 marks per point developed. For example: A Christian believer might agree that the complexity of the natural world points to God as its designer, as Paley argued in his watchmaker analogy (1), because the intricate structure of organisms like the human eye seems too complex to have arisen without purpose (2). By contrast, an atheist might argue that Darwin's theory of evolution explains biological complexity through natural selection without needing a designer (1), so apparent design in nature is not evidence of God (2).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some people find the argument from miracles convincing as evidence for God's existence.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, each showing how the argument from miracles supports belief in God. A relevant source is named and used well. For example: the resurrection of Jesus in Luke 24 as an event that defies natural explanation and requires a divine cause; and the healings at Lourdes where the Catholic Church has recognised medically inexplicable recoveries. Sub-tradition contrast or reference to multiple religious traditions present. Response engages with why the miracle counts as evidence. Secure: Two relevant reasons given, source referenced but not fully developed; explanation present on each point. Developing: One or two points stated without development; source absent or very vague ('the Bible'). Emerging: Basic point only; largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Priya is a 16-year-old Hindu student debating philosophy of religion with her sceptical friend Callum. Callum says the Design argument is the strongest reason to believe in God. Priya is unsure. Give two reasons Callum might use to support his view.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for each reason stated, 2 marks for each reason developed. For example: Callum might point to the extraordinary complexity of living organisms, such as the structure of DNA, which appears to be too ordered to have arisen by chance (1) — this is what Paley's watchmaker analogy illustrates: as a watch implies a watchmaker, a complex universe implies a designer (2). He might also argue that the fine-tuning of physical constants in the universe (the fact that if gravity or nuclear forces were slightly different, life would be impossible) seems to point to deliberate design (1), suggesting there must be an intelligence behind the universe (2).

practice_questions.text:
'The Design argument is the best evidence for the existence of God.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious and non-religious views
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: The Design argument draws on observable evidence that is accessible to everyone, not just believers. Paley's watchmaker analogy powerfully conveys the intuition that order implies a designer. Genesis 1:31 describes God as the intentional creator of a good, ordered universe. Many scientists such as Swinburne have developed the fine-tuning version of the argument, suggesting physical constants are calibrated for life. For believers, the argument confirms what they already hold through faith: that God is the creative intelligence behind all things.

Arguments against: Hume argued the analogy between a watch and the universe is weak, and that poor design in nature (disease, natural disasters) might suggest an incompetent or uncaring designer. Darwin's theory of evolution demonstrated that biological complexity can arise through natural selection without a designer. Atheists and humanists argue that scientific explanation makes the God hypothesis unnecessary. The First Cause argument or the argument from miracles may be more direct routes to God's existence for some thinkers, suggesting the Design argument is not the strongest available.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation with at least two developed arguments on each side, reference to religious sources (Genesis 1, Paley, Aquinas) and non-religious views (Hume, Darwin, atheism/humanism), and a justified conclusion stating which side is stronger and why. Secure: Most key points present; source reference partially developed; conclusion reached but not fully justified. Developing: One-sided or points listed without evaluation; limited source use; conclusion absent or undeveloped. Emerging: Basic description with little evaluation; no conclusion.

lessons.title: Arguments Against the Existence of God
lessons.description: Evil, suffering and science as arguments against God, with Christian, Muslim, Jewish, atheist and humanist responses.
lessons.content_html:
Does Suffering Challenge Belief in God?

If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and entirely good, why does suffering exist? This question — known as the problem of evil — is one of the oldest and most persistent arguments against the existence of God. Alongside it, the findings of modern science have been used to argue that a creator God is unnecessary. Together, these represent the most serious challenges that believers must respond to. This lesson examines both challenges and the responses that religious traditions offer.

Types of Evil and Suffering

Philosophers distinguish two types of evil. Natural evil includes suffering caused by events like earthquakes, tsunamis, cancer, and famine — things that happen regardless of human action. Moral evil refers to suffering caused by human choices: war, genocide, abuse, cruelty. The philosopher J.L. Mackie argued in his 1955 essay “Evil and Omnipotence” that the existence of evil is logically inconsistent with an all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good God. If God is able to prevent evil (omnipotence), knows about evil (omniscience) and wants to prevent it (omnibenevolence), then evil should not exist. Its existence, Mackie argued, means at least one of those divine attributes must be false — or God does not exist.

Key Fact

Natural evil = suffering from nature (earthquakes, disease). Moral evil = suffering from human choices (war, murder). J.L. Mackie argued that the existence of either type is logically inconsistent with a God who is omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing) and omnibenevolent (all-good).

Christian Responses to the Problem of Evil

Christian theology has developed several responses to the problem of evil. The soul-making theodicy — associated with the philosopher John Hick and drawing on the early Christian thinker Irenaeus — argues that God permits suffering because it is the necessary condition for human moral and spiritual growth. Just as muscles strengthen through resistance, character develops through challenge. A world without suffering would be a world without the opportunity to develop courage, compassion, or perseverance. Irenaeus described humanity as made “in the image of God” but not yet fully in the “likeness of God” — suffering is part of the journey towards that likeness.

The free will defence — developed by Alvin Plantinga — argues that God created humans with genuine freedom to choose between good and evil. Moral evil is the result of people misusing that freedom. A world in which God prevented every act of evil would require removing human free will, and a world of puppets doing only what God programmes them to do would have less moral worth than a world of genuinely free agents. Many Christians draw on Genesis 3 (the Fall) to explain how human sin entered the world through Adam and Eve’s free choice to disobey God.

In Islam, suffering is understood within the framework of qadar (divine decree). Muslims hold that God is entirely just and that all suffering ultimately serves God’s purposes, even when humans cannot understand them. Suffering is seen as a test from God: “We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits” (Qur’an 2:155). Patient endurance (sabr) in the face of suffering is itself a form of worship. Islam also emphasises that natural evil does not originate from a devil equal to God — there is no dualism; God alone is ultimate.

In Jewish tradition, the problem of suffering is powerfully explored in the Book of Job. Job is a righteous man who loses everything — family, health, wealth — not as punishment for sin but as a test. Job’s response is to continue trusting God even when he cannot understand why he suffers. Jewish theology does not offer a single theodicy but encourages wrestling with the question honestly. After the Holocaust, many Jewish thinkers such as Elie Wiesel and Emil Fackenheim engaged deeply with the question of how God could permit such suffering, with varying conclusions about faith and protest.

Arguments Based on Science

Alongside the problem of evil, modern science has provided alternative accounts of the universe’s origin and development that some argue make the existence of a creator God unnecessary. The Big Bang theory, developed through the work of Georges Lemaître, Edwin Hubble and others in the 20th century, describes the universe as originating in an extraordinarily rapid expansion from an extremely dense initial state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. This is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: the observed expansion of the universe, the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the relative abundance of light elements.

Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection, set out in On the Origin of Species (1859), explained how the diversity and complexity of living organisms developed over billions of years through random variation and the survival of the fittest. Atheist scientists and philosophers such as Richard Dawkins argue that evolution removes the need for a designer God: once we understand how complex life arises through natural selection, the Design argument loses its force. The universe, on this view, is explicable entirely in terms of natural causes.

Many students write that “science has proved God does not exist.” This is inaccurate and loses marks. Science describes how the universe operates through natural processes; it cannot, in principle, disprove the existence of a being outside or beyond the universe. What science does is remove the necessity of a God-explanation for specific things — the origin of species, the age of the Earth — by providing natural explanations. Many religious believers, including the Catholic Church (which teaches that evolution and Big Bang cosmology are compatible with belief in God as creator), accept the findings of science while continuing to believe. The debate between science and religion is more nuanced than a simple clash.

Atheist and Humanist Perspectives

For atheists, the combination of the problem of evil and scientific explanation makes belief in God unnecessary and unjustified. The ancient Greek formulation attributed to Epicurus is still quoted: if God is willing to prevent evil but unable, God is not omnipotent; if God is able but unwilling, God is not good; if God is both willing and able, why does evil exist? Bertrand Russell famously stated that there is no sufficient reason to believe in God and that the problem of evil in particular makes the idea of a benevolent creator implausible.

Humanism, as represented in the UK by Humanists UK, holds that human beings can live ethical, meaningful lives through reason, compassion and humanity alone, without the need for religious belief or a divine lawgiver. Humanists do not regard the problem of evil as a dilemma they need to resolve — they simply do not begin with the assumption that an all-powerful, all-good God exists. For humanists, suffering is a natural fact of a universe governed by physical laws, and the appropriate response is human solidarity and action to reduce suffering, not prayer or theodicy.

Key Fact

The free will defence: God gave humans genuine freedom to choose; moral evil is humans misusing that freedom, not God’s fault. Counter-argument: free will does not explain natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — these are not caused by human choice.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark ‘Explain two reasons’ question on evil and suffering, many students forget to name a source of religious teaching. For this topic, strong sources include: Genesis 3 (the Fall — free will defence), Job (Jewish response to suffering), Qur’an 2:155 (Islamic view of suffering as a test), or the teaching of Irenaeus/John Hick (soul-making theodicy). Simply saying “Christians believe God has reasons” without naming a tradition, thinker or source will keep your answer in the Developing band. Name the thinker AND link their idea back to the question.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, a common mistake is writing only about why evil is a problem for belief in God and ignoring the responses. Top-band answers present the problem (Mackie’s logical argument), then explain and evaluate the responses (free will, soul-making, the distinction between natural and moral evil), include non-religious views (atheism, humanism), and reach a justified conclusion: “I conclude that the problem of evil is a serious challenge, but believers may find the free will defence and the soul-making theodicy sufficient responses because...”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The problem of evil (J.L. Mackie) argues that natural evil and moral evil are logically inconsistent with a God who is omnipotent, omniscient and omnibenevolent. Christian responses include the free will defence (Plantinga) and the soul-making theodicy (Hick/Irenaeus).
  • Islamic theology sees suffering as a test from God requiring patient endurance (sabr); Jewish tradition (the Book of Job) emphasises honest wrestling with the question of suffering while maintaining trust in God.
  • Scientific arguments (Big Bang theory, Darwin’s evolution) offer natural explanations for the universe and life, removing the need for a creator God in the view of atheists and humanists; many believers, however, consider science and faith compatible.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes natural evil?
A) Suffering caused by human choices such as war and murder
B) Suffering caused by natural events such as earthquakes and disease
C) The belief that evil is an illusion created by the mind
D) The view that God created evil to test humanity
practice_questions.marks: B) Suffering caused by natural events such as earthquakes and disease [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one argument used by atheists against the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of the following accepted for 1 mark: the problem of evil (1); the argument from science / evolution / Big Bang (1); the absence of evidence for God (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two contrasting beliefs about why God permits suffering.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark per belief stated, 2 marks per belief developed. For example: The free will defence holds that God permits moral evil because he gave humans genuine freedom to choose between good and evil (1), and removing suffering would mean removing human freedom, which would make humans into puppets rather than genuine moral agents (2). By contrast, the soul-making theodicy holds that God permits suffering because it is necessary for humans to develop virtues like courage and compassion (1); a life without challenges would not allow people to grow morally and spiritually towards the likeness of God, as Irenaeus described (2).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some people argue that science makes belief in God unnecessary.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons with sources used effectively. For example: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection (On the Origin of Species, 1859) showed that the complexity of living organisms can arise through natural processes, removing the need for a designer God that the Design argument assumed (developed reason 1). The Big Bang theory provides a scientific account of the origin of the universe without requiring a creator, supported by evidence such as the expansion of the universe and cosmic microwave background radiation (developed reason 2). Source(s) from religious or philosophical tradition used accurately and linked to the argument. Secure: Two relevant reasons; source present but not fully developed. Developing: One developed reason, or two undeveloped; source vague. Emerging: Basic point only; no source.

practice_questions.text: Layla is a 15-year-old Muslim student whose family has recently experienced a serious illness. Her Christian friend Ethan says suffering proves there is no God. Give two reasons Layla might use to respond from an Islamic perspective.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark per reason stated, 2 marks per reason developed. For example: Layla might say that Islam teaches suffering is a test from God (1); the Qur'an (2:155) says 'We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss' and that patient endurance (sabr) in the face of such tests is a form of worship (2). She might also say that Muslims believe God is entirely just, and that suffering serves God's purposes even when humans cannot understand them (1); unlike Ethan's view, Islamic theology does not see suffering as incompatible with God's goodness because God's perspective encompasses all of time and eternity (2).

practice_questions.text:
'The problem of evil proves that God does not exist.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious and non-religious views
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: J.L. Mackie argued in 'Evil and Omnipotence' that the existence of evil is logically inconsistent with an omnipotent, omniscient, omnibenevolent God. Natural evil (earthquakes, cancer) is not caused by human free will, so the free will defence cannot explain it. Atheists argue that a loving God would prevent innocent suffering if able to do so. Richard Dawkins contends that evolution removes any need for a creator and that the universe shows no sign of benevolent design.

Arguments against: The free will defence (Plantinga) argues moral evil results from human freedom, which God values; removing evil would require removing freedom. The soul-making theodicy (Hick/Irenaeus) holds that suffering is necessary for moral growth; Genesis 3 (the Fall) provides a scriptural account of how sin entered the world. Many believers point out that the problem of evil is a dilemma only if God's existence is assumed first; in themselves, suffering and evil do not logically disprove God's existence, they only challenge certain descriptions of God. The Book of Job shows that honest wrestling with suffering can coexist with faith. The Catholic Church teaches that evolution and the Big Bang are compatible with belief in God as creator.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation, at least two points on each side fully developed, religious sources used (Genesis 3, Qur'an 2:155, Job), non-religious view (Mackie, atheism, humanism) engaged with, justified conclusion. Secure: Main arguments present; conclusion reached but weighing incomplete. Developing: One-sided or points listed; conclusion absent or undeveloped. Emerging: Descriptive; no real evaluation or conclusion.

lessons.title: Revelation: Visions, Miracles and Nature
lessons.description: Special and general revelation, visions, enlightenment, divine attributes, and challenges to religious experience.
lessons.content_html:
How Do People Claim to Know God?

If God exists, how might humans gain knowledge of this? Religious traditions across the world describe two broad paths: special revelation and general revelation. Both have been used to describe divine attributes — the qualities believers ascribe to God. Both have also been challenged by philosophers and non-believers. This lesson explores what these terms mean, what they reveal about the divine, and why their value is contested.

Special Revelation: Visions

Special revelation refers to direct, personal experiences in which God (or, in non-theistic traditions, ultimate reality) is believed to communicate with a specific individual. One of the most commonly cited forms is the vision. Visions are reported across religious traditions. In Christianity, the conversion of Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) is a classic example: Saul was travelling to persecute Christians when a blinding light surrounded him and he heard the voice of Jesus. After this experience, he became Paul the Apostle and one of the most significant figures in early Christianity. Believers regard this as a direct encounter with the risen Christ — a special revelation that transformed an individual’s life and understanding.

The Marian apparitions at Lourdes in 1858 offer a second example. The 14-year-old Bernadette Soubirous reported seeing a vision of a luminous woman at the grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes who identified herself as “the Immaculate Conception.” The Catholic Church, after extensive investigation, officially recognised the apparitions in 1862. The site of Lourdes has since become one of the world’s most visited pilgrimage destinations, and the healings reported there are subject to scrutiny by a medical bureau. For Catholics, Bernadette’s vision is a genuine revelation — a direct communication from the divine to a human being.

Key Fact

Two widely cited examples of visions: (1) Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) — a blinding light and the voice of Jesus led to Saul’s conversion and transformation into Paul the Apostle. (2) Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes (1858) — visions of the Virgin Mary, recognised by the Catholic Church, that established Lourdes as a major pilgrimage site.

Special Revelation: Enlightenment

Enlightenment is a distinct category of special revelation that appears across several traditions. In Buddhism, the Bodhi (awakening) of Siddhartha Gautama under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya is the paradigmatic example. The Buddha did not receive a revelation from a creator God — Buddhism does not require belief in such a God — but he attained a direct insight into the nature of reality: the Four Noble Truths and the way to end suffering. This is significant for Theme C because it illustrates how the idea of “revelation” operates differently in different traditions. For Buddhists, enlightenment is the direct realisation of truth about existence, not a message from a divine person.

In Sikh teaching, the founder Guru Nanak received a revelation from Waheguru (God) when he went to bathe in a river and did not return for three days. When he emerged, he declared: “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” Sikhs understand this as a direct divine revelation that formed the foundation of the Sikh path. The Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal Sikh scripture, is itself understood as the living word of God — revelation in written form. In Hindu mystical traditions such as Advaita Vedanta, the highest form of enlightenment (moksha) involves the direct experiential realisation that atman (the individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one.

General Revelation: Nature and Scripture

Unlike special revelation (which comes to specific individuals), general revelation is available to all people through the natural world and through reason. Many believers hold that the beauty and order of nature — the turning of seasons, the complexity of the cell, the vastness of the cosmos — communicates something about its creator. The Christian theologian Thomas Aquinas believed that natural reason could arrive at some knowledge of God through the created order, even without scripture. The Qur’an calls the natural world “ayat” (signs) of God’s existence and power: “In the creation of the heavens and earth... there are signs for those who reason” (Qur’an 3:190). Genesis 1 presents God as deliberately ordering creation: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31), suggesting that creation itself reflects God’s character.

Scripture is another form of general revelation that believers across traditions regard as a source of knowledge about the divine. The Christian Bible, the Qur’an, the Torah, and the Guru Granth Sahib are each regarded by their respective communities as containing revealed knowledge of God’s nature, will and purposes. For many believers, scripture provides a more reliable and systematic form of knowledge about God than individual mystical experience, precisely because it is accessible to all and tested by a community over time.

Religious traditions describe the divine using several key attributes. An omnipotent God has unlimited power — a quality supported by accounts of miracles and by the creation narratives in Genesis, the Qur’an and the Guru Granth Sahib. An omniscient God knows all things, including the deepest thoughts of every human being — present in Psalm 139 (“You have searched me, Lord, and you know me”) and in Islamic teaching about God’s omniscience (al-Alim).

Theistic traditions also distinguish between a personal God — one who cares for individuals, hears prayer, and acts in history — and an impersonal divine — an ultimate reality or force that does not relate to humans as a person. Many Hindu schools understand Brahman as ultimately impersonal: the ground of all existence, not a deity with feelings or intentions. Buddhism similarly does not teach a personal creator God. By contrast, Christianity, Islam, Judaism and Sikhism all describe God in strongly personal terms.

A immanent God is present within the world and within human experience: active in history, responsive to prayer, encountered in worship. A transcendent God exists beyond and above the universe: unlimited by space, time or matter. Most monotheistic traditions hold that God is both — “closer to you than your jugular vein” (Qur’an 50:16) and yet beyond full human comprehension. The tension between divine immanence and transcendence is a central theme in the philosophy of religion.

Challenges to Revelation as a Source of Knowledge

Not everyone accepts that visions, miracles and religious experiences are genuine sources of knowledge about the divine. Several challenges deserve careful consideration. First, different revelatory experiences lead to contradictory conclusions about the divine — some describe a personal God, others an impersonal ultimate reality, others a universe without any creator at all. If revelation were a reliable source of knowledge, we might expect greater agreement. Philosophers such as John Hick have grappled with this, arguing that all religious experiences may be culturally shaped encounters with the same ultimate reality.

Second, there is always the possibility that those who claim to have had visions or miraculous experiences were lying or mistaken. Hume argued that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and personal testimony — especially from centuries ago — does not meet this standard. Modern psychology offers natural explanations for mystical experiences: they may result from unusual brain states, sensory deprivation, grief, or temporal lobe activity. The philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach argued that “God” is a human projection — what we value most in ourselves, projected onto the cosmos.

Humanists and atheists typically hold that reported visions and religious experiences, however sincere, do not provide reliable evidence of an objective divine reality. They point out that the specific content of religious experiences consistently reflects the cultural background of the person having them — a medieval Christian is unlikely to report an encounter with Waheguru, and a devout Sikh is unlikely to report seeing the Virgin Mary. This cultural conditioning, non-religious thinkers argue, suggests the experience originates in the human mind rather than in an external divine source. The appropriate response to claims of special revelation is, on this view, respectful scepticism and a search for natural explanations.

Key Fact

Four key divine attributes: omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), immanent (present within the world and in human experience), transcendent (beyond and above the universe). Most monotheistic traditions — Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Sikhism — hold that God is all four simultaneously. Some Hindu schools and Buddhist teachings describe the divine as impersonal rather than personal.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark Explain question for this topic, a common mistake is confusing special and general revelation. Special revelation is direct and personal — a vision, a miracle, enlightenment. General revelation is indirect and universal — available to all through nature and scripture. You must be clear about which one you are describing. Always name a specific example of a vision (Saul on the road to Damascus, Acts 9; or Bernadette at Lourdes) and use it to explain WHY it counts as a source of knowledge about the divine. Remember to refer to a sacred writing or source of teaching — Acts 9, Qur’an 3:190, Genesis 1:31, or the Guru Granth Sahib are all strong sources for this lesson.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, make sure you engage with both sides of the argument about whether revelation is a reliable source of knowledge. Arguments for its value should reference believers’ experiences and their significance; arguments against should include Hume’s point about testimony, the cultural conditioning critique, and the possibility of natural (psychological) explanations. Your conclusion must say which side you find more persuasive, and why, with explicit reasoning.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Special revelation involves direct, personal encounters with the divine: visions (Saul on the road to Damascus, Acts 9; Bernadette at Lourdes) and enlightenment (the Buddha at Bodh Gaya; Guru Nanak’s revelation). These are understood differently across traditions — Buddhism’s enlightenment does not require a creator God.
  • General revelation — through nature and scripture (Genesis 1:31, Qur’an 3:190, Guru Granth Sahib) — is available to all and reveals divine attributes: omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), immanent (present in the world) and transcendent (beyond the universe).
  • Challenges include: contradictory revelations across traditions, the possibility that witnesses were lying or mistaken (Hume), psychological explanations for religious experiences, and the humanist view that religious experiences originate in the human mind rather than in an external divine source.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'general revelation'?
A) A personal vision or miracle experienced by one individual
B) Knowledge of God available to all through the natural world and scripture
C) The Buddhist teaching of enlightenment under the Bodhi tree
D) A direct communication from God to a specific prophet
practice_questions.marks: B) Knowledge of God available to all through the natural world and scripture [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one example of a vision from the Christian tradition.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of the following accepted for 1 mark: Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) (1); Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes (1858) (1); the Virgin Mary appearing to Bernadette (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two contrasting ideas about whether God is personal or impersonal.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark per idea stated, 2 marks per idea developed. For example: Most Christian, Muslim, Jewish and Sikh traditions describe God as personal — a being who hears prayer, acts in history and cares for individuals (1); this is supported by texts such as Psalm 139 ('You have searched me, Lord, and you know me') which present God as intimately involved in individual human lives (2). By contrast, some Hindu schools such as Advaita Vedanta describe Brahman as ultimately impersonal — the ground of all existence without personal characteristics such as feelings or intentions (1); on this view, the highest spiritual goal is realising that the individual self (atman) is one with Brahman, rather than entering a personal relationship with a deity (2).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some believers find visions a convincing source of knowledge about God.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, each explaining why visions count as convincing evidence of God. At least one specific vision example named and linked to a sacred text or source of authority. For example: reason 1 — the dramatic transformation of the person who had the vision (Saul/Paul in Acts 9 became the founding apostle of Christianity, a change so radical that believers see it as requiring a genuine divine cause); reason 2 — the corroborating physical evidence in some cases (the healings at Lourdes, recognised by medical scrutiny, suggest that something beyond natural explanation is occurring). Source(s) named and developed. Secure: Two relevant reasons; source referenced but partially developed. Developing: One reason developed; source vague or absent. Emerging: Basic point only; largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Tariq, a 17-year-old Muslim student, tells his Religious Studies class that he thinks the natural world is the best evidence for God. His classmate Rosa says she finds personal visions more convincing. Explain two reasons Tariq might give for his view.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark per reason stated, 2 marks per reason developed. For example: Tariq might argue that general revelation through nature is available to everyone, not just those who happen to have a vision (1); the Qur'an (3:190) says that in the creation of the heavens and earth 'there are signs for those who reason', suggesting that God intentionally made the natural world a source of knowledge accessible to all humanity (2). He might also argue that personal visions could be explained by psychology or cultural expectation (1), whereas the existence of the ordered universe is an objective fact that cannot be dismissed as an individual's subjective experience (2).

practice_questions.text:
'Visions and religious experiences are not a reliable source of knowledge about God.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious and non-religious views
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Hume argued that it is always more probable a witness was mistaken or lying than that a miracle or vision genuinely occurred. Visions in different religious traditions produce contradictory descriptions of God (personal/impersonal, one God/many gods), suggesting they cannot all be accurate. Modern psychology can explain mystical experiences through unusual brain states, sensory deprivation or grief, without invoking the supernatural. Humanists and atheists argue that the content of religious experiences reflects the cultural background of the person, suggesting human origin rather than divine revelation.

Arguments against: Many who have had visions report life-transforming changes that are hard to explain naturally — Saul's conversion (Acts 9) is cited as evidence that something objective occurred. The Catholic Church subjects miracle claims at Lourdes to rigorous medical scrutiny before recognising them, and 70 have been recognised. General revelation through nature is corroborated by independent evidence across cultures and traditions. Many philosophers (William Alston, Alvin Plantinga) argue that religious experience is epistemically justified — just as we trust sense perception as a source of knowledge about the world, we may be justified in trusting religious experience. The Guru Granth Sahib and other scriptures represent tested, communal forms of revelation rather than idiosyncratic personal claims.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation; at least two points on each side developed; sources used (Acts 9, Qur'an 3:190, Genesis 1:31); non-religious views engaged with; justified conclusion present. Secure: Main points present; source referenced but not fully developed; conclusion reached but weighing incomplete. Developing: One-sided; limited source use; conclusion absent. Emerging: Descriptive only; no evaluation or conclusion.

glossary_terms.definition: Direct, personal communication or experience of God or ultimate reality, such as a vision, miracle or moment of enlightenment.
Indirect knowledge of God available to all people through the natural world, reason and scripture, rather than through a direct personal encounter.
A supernatural experience in which a person believes they see or hear God, a divine being, or a messenger of God.
A profound experience of direct insight into ultimate reality; in Buddhism, the awakening of the Buddha; in other traditions, a direct experience of union with or knowledge of God.
All-powerful; able to do anything that is logically possible; one of the key attributes ascribed to God in monotheistic religions.
All-knowing; having complete knowledge of all things, past, present and future.
A description of God as present within the world and within human experience, active in history and in individuals' lives.
A description of God as existing beyond and above the physical universe, not limited by space, time or matter.
A description of God as a being with whom humans can have a personal relationship, who cares for individuals and responds to prayer.
